A sample $S\subset U$ of size $n$ is observed; write $R=U\setminus S$ for the $N-n$ non-sampled units. The targets are $$ T=\sum_{i\in U}Y_i,\qquad \bar Y_U=T/N . $$ The prediction approach treats $Y_1,\dots,Y_N$ as random variables generated by a model $\xi$, and treats $S$ as fixed. All expectations below are with respect to $\xi$, not with respect to the randomization distribution. The role of simple random sampling is only to guarantee that selection carries no information about $Y_i$, so that the model assumed for the sampled units also holds for the non-sampled ones. Throughout, the working model is $$ \xi:\quad E(Y_i)=\mu,\quad \operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\sigma^2,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)=0\ (i\ne j). $$ {#eq-model} It is convenient to write the model errors as $$ e_i=Y_i-\mu,\qquad E(e_i)=0,\quad \operatorname{Var}(e_i)=\sigma^2,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(e_i,e_j)=0\ (i\ne j), $$ {#eq-errors} and $\bar e_A=|A|^{-1}\sum_{i\in A}e_i$ for any index set $A$. Every derivation below proceeds by subtracting and adding $\mu$ so that the prediction error is expressed in the $e_i$, whose moments are given by @eq-errors. Any predictor of $T$ has the form $\hat T=\sum_{i\in U}\hat Y_i$, and its accuracy is measured by the **mean squared prediction error** $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat T)=E\left[\left(\hat T-T\right)^{2}\right] =E\left[\left(\sum_{i\in U}(\hat Y_i-Y_i)\right)^{2}\right]. $$ {#eq-mspe} The name matters: $T$ is a random quantity to be predicted, not a fixed parameter to be estimated, so @eq-mspe measures prediction error rather than estimation error. ### Known $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ {#sec-pred-known-mu} Suppose $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are known and we set $\hat Y_i=\mu$ for every $i\in U$, ignoring the observed data. Then $\hat T=N\mu$, and subtracting and adding $\mu$ inside each term gives $$ \hat T-T=\sum_{i\in U}\left(\mu-Y_i\right)=-\sum_{i\in U}\left(Y_i-\mu\right)=-\sum_{i\in U}e_i . $$ The prediction error is a sum of zero-mean model errors, so $\hat T$ is model-unbiased, and $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat T)=E\left[\left(\sum_{i\in U}e_i\right)^{2}\right] =\sum_{i\in U}E(e_i^2)+\sum_{i\ne j}E(e_ie_j)=N\sigma^2 , $$ {#eq-mspe-blind} the cross-products vanishing by @eq-errors. For the population mean, $\hat{\bar y}_U=\mu$ gives $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat{\bar y}_U)=\frac{\sigma^2}{N}. $$ Two points deserve emphasis. First, the error is not zero even though the model is known exactly: $T$ is a realized sum of random variables, so it cannot be recovered from $\mu$ alone. This is the essential difference between predicting a finite-population quantity and estimating a superpopulation parameter. Second, $\sigma^2/N$ is negligible for large $N$, which is why the distinction is usually invisible in treatments that condition on the population. The predictor $N\mu$ is nonetheless wasteful, since it predicts $Y_i$ for units whose values we have already seen. Replacing $\hat Y_i$ by $Y_i$ for $i\in S$ gives $$ \hat T=\sum_{i\in S}Y_i+(N-n)\mu,\qquad \hat T-T=\sum_{i\in R}\left(\mu-Y_i\right)=-\sum_{i\in R}e_i , $$ so that $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat T)=(N-n)\sigma^2 . $$ {#eq-mspe-oracle} The $n$ observed terms have simply dropped out. Expression @eq-mspe-oracle is the irreducible part of the problem: the unobserved units vary about their mean, and no predictor can remove that variation. The result of the next section is @eq-mspe-oracle plus a penalty for not knowing $\mu$. ### Unknown $\mu$: prediction by the sample mean {#sec-pred-sample-mean} Now let $\mu$ be unknown and estimate it by $\bar y_S=n^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}Y_i$. Take $$ \hat Y_i= \begin{cases} Y_i, & i\in S,\\ \bar y_S, & i\in R, \end{cases} \qquad\text{so that}\qquad \hat T=\sum_{i\in S}Y_i+(N-n)\bar y_S=N\bar y_S . $$ {#eq-expansion} The familiar expansion estimator thus arises as a predictor, not as a design-unbiased estimator. Its prediction error involves only the non-sampled units, and subtracting and adding $\mu$ in each term separates the two sources of error: $$ \hat T-T=\sum_{i\in R}\left(\bar y_S-Y_i\right) =\sum_{i\in R}\Big\{\underbrace{(\bar y_S-\mu)}_{\bar e_S}-\underbrace{(Y_i-\mu)}_{e_i}\Big\} =(N-n)\,\bar e_S-\sum_{i\in R}e_i . $$ {#eq-error-decomp} The first term in @eq-error-decomp is the error made in locating $\mu$ from the sample; the second is the intrinsic scatter of the unobserved units about $\mu$. Both have mean zero, so $\hat T$ is model-unbiased. Squaring and taking expectations, $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat T)=(N-n)^2E\left(\bar e_S^{\,2}\right) -2(N-n)E\left(\bar e_S\sum_{i\in R}e_i\right) +E\left[\left(\sum_{i\in R}e_i\right)^{2}\right]. $$ The three terms are evaluated separately. Since $E(\bar e_S^{\,2})=\sigma^2/n$, the first equals $(N-n)^2\sigma^2/n$. The cross term vanishes because $S$ and $R$ are disjoint, so every product $e_ie_j$ appearing in it has $i\ne j$. The third equals $(N-n)\sigma^2$, again by @eq-errors. Hence $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat T)=\frac{(N-n)^2}{n}\sigma^2+(N-n)\sigma^2 =(N-n)\sigma^2\left(\frac{N-n}{n}+1\right) =\frac{N(N-n)}{n}\,\sigma^2 , $$ {#eq-mspe-total} and, dividing by $N^2$, $$ \operatorname{MSPE}(\hat{\bar y}_U)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\left(1-\frac{n}{N}\right). $$ {#eq-mspe-mean} Expression @eq-mspe-mean is the classical simple-random-sampling variance, with the superpopulation variance $\sigma^2$ in place of the population variance $S^2$, obtained without any appeal to randomization. Three features are worth drawing out. The two components of @eq-mspe-total have distinct meanings. The term $(N-n)\sigma^2$ is the irreducible variation identified in @eq-mspe-oracle; the term $(N-n)^2\sigma^2/n$ is the price of estimating $\mu$ from $n$ observations, and it alone shrinks as $n$ grows. The finite-population correction is not an artifact of sampling without replacement. It emerges from the arithmetic of a census of $S$: the $n$ observed units contribute exactly zero to @eq-error-decomp, so only $N-n$ terms remain to be predicted. When $n=N$ the MSPE is zero because nothing is left to predict. Finally, comparing @eq-mspe-total with @eq-mspe-oracle, the cost of not knowing $\mu$ is the factor $N/n$. For the population mean, the MSPE rises from $\sigma^2/N$ to approximately $\sigma^2/n$; the sample size, not the population size, governs precision. A natural next step is to estimate $\sigma^2$ by the sample variance $s_S^2$ and to verify that $E(s_S^2)=\sigma^2$ under @eq-model, which yields the usual variance estimator and closes the loop with the design-based formulas.
